content: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) is a frequent complication observed in preterm infants. This condition is associated with adverse long-term respiratory and neurodevelopmental outcomes, as well as an increased risk of mortality. Pentoxifylline, a synthetic methylxanthine and phosphodiesterase inhibitor, has been proposed as a potential prophylactic agent to reduce the incidence of BPD due to its anti-inflammatory properties. The primary aim of this review was to evaluate the effect of pentoxifylline on the incidence of BPD, death before 36 weeks postmenstrual age (PMA), and the combined outcome of BPD or death before 36 weeks PMA in preterm neonates. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, EMBASE, PubMed, and CINAHL, covering studies published up to September 2012. Additionally, references and cross-references from identified studies were reviewed, and abstracts from Pediatric Academic Societies Meetings (1990–2012) were hand-searched. No language restrictions were applied. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized or quasi-randomized clinical trials involving systemic or nebulized pentoxifylline in preterm neonates born at less than 32 weeks of gestation or weighing less than 1500 grams at birth. Eligible studies needed to report at least one relevant outcome. Standard Cochrane methods were employed for data collection and analysis, with two independent reviewers selecting studies and resolving disagreements through discussion. Only one randomized clinical trial met the inclusion criteria. This study compared nebulized pentoxifylline with a placebo in 100 preterm infants for the prevention of BPD. However, the trial was deemed to have a high risk of bias due to the lack of blinding of both the intervention and outcome assessors, as well as incomplete outcome data. The results showed no statistically significant difference between nebulized pentoxifylline and placebo in reducing the incidence of BPD at 36 weeks PMA or death before 36 weeks PMA. Furthermore, there was no significant effect on secondary outcomes such as intraventricular hemorrhage, periventricular leukomalacia, sepsis, or patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) requiring surgical ligation. The study did not report on other secondary outcomes or long-term outcomes, and the reporting of adverse events was insufficient to allow for reliable conclusions regarding safety. In conclusion, the current evidence is insufficient to determine the safety and efficacy of pentoxifylline for the prevention of BPD in preterm neonates. The authors recommend that further clinical trials be conducted to clarify the role of pentoxifylline in this context. These trials should focus on clinically significant outcomes and ideally include long-term neurodevelopmental follow-up.
